newsitem.title: USA: Firm looks to securitize lottery winnings.
newsitem.headline: Firm looks to securitize lottery winnings.

text.p: Securitize it and they will come. That's what bankers at Woodbridge Sterling Capital LLC hope as they serve up the first bond offering which pools future cash flows of winning lottery tickets.

At least one firm currently offers lottery winners the chance to cash in all or part of their winnings rather than making them wait over a period of several years to collect the full winnings. The new twist is that Woodbridge will purchase multiple winning lottery tickets at a discount and pool them to create a new form of asset-backed security.

"The lottery winner assigns the lottery winnings to Woodbridge so they do not have to wait five years to get their payment," said Michael Damore, general counsel at Woodbridge, a New York-based firm, which purchases winning lottery ticket cash flows. "We do business with people who want cash now."

The first securitization is expected to come to market in October, as a multi-tranche deal that will pool cash flows from about 80 winning lottery tickets. The pool of winning lottery cash flows could include a wide range of winners: holders of $50,000 tickets to those with a $40 million winning ticket.

Early price talk for the offering, which has sparked some investor interest, is that the deal will price at 120 to 130 basis points over U.S. Treasury securities with maturities comprable to the average life of the assets being pooled.
Noting that most lottery grand prizes of $1 million or more are paid out over 20 years, Damore said the service could benefit older lottery winners who want more cash up front.

For instance, Damore said, a $1 million ticket winner can get an immediate payment of $585,000 to $590,000 before taxes given current interest rates. But he said most winners would probably take some payments in the future.
"Most people sell a piece of future payments to generate cash now and continue to get future payments," said Damore.
The first sale of future lottery winning cash flows may have been as early as 1989, but, Damore said the business of selling future cashflows from lottery tickets began in earnest by 1993.
"We estimate that in excess of $400 million of lottery receivables have been purchased by institutional investors in the last four years," said Damore.

The investors who have proven to be most keen on purchasing these future receivables are insurance companies. The securities based on pooled lottery winnings are expected to be snapped up by insurers as well.
PNC Capital Markets Inc said it expects to place $20 million in these special asset-backed securities and has provided a $30 million line of credit with which to purchase the lottery cash flows.
Other institutional investors who may buy this type of offering include pension funds, said John McElravey, vice president in the asset backed group at Duff & Phelps Credit Rating Co.

"The credit quality of the obligor, which is the state or its lottery commission, is pretty good," said McElravey. He added that states which allow the assignment of lottery winnings to another party are single-A rated or better.

The securitization allows for a more efficient sale of the future cashflows. While insurers bought transactions -- that is lottery ticket cash flows -- one at a time, the pooling of these cash flows is expected to broaden the investor base.
The pools of lotteries, said Damore, will be serviced and rated. The expected first transaction in October should total $20 million and will be structured as a 144A private placement.

Not all states allow winners to assign their winnings to other parties. According to McElravey, 15 states explicitly allow for the assignment of lottery ticket winnings to another party -- among them New York, Pennsylvania and California -- while others do not have a clear policy.
